extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in X/Twitter platform history and policies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the platform policies, moderation practices, legal controversies, and content/verification standards described on the Wikipedia article about Twitter (rebranded X). Useful for understanding how the service handled bots, misinformation, pornography, government requests, and community moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account suspension for QAnon-associated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter suspended more than 70,000 accounts for sharing "harmful QAnon-associated content" at large scale and dedicated to propagation of this conspiracy theory across the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspensions were applied where accounts were assessed to be engaged in large‑scale propagation and dedicated promotion of the conspiracy theory; example includes suspension of then‑President Trump's account and later settlement related to that suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of state-linked fake/malicious accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter identified and removed thousands of fake accounts attributed to state influence operations (e.g., >7,000 Iranian fake accounts; 5,929 accounts tied to a Saudi Arabia operation; ~3,500 fake accounts influencing American audiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removals were based on detection of coordinated, inauthentic, or spammy behavior attributed to foreign state operations; Twitter sometimes reported partial counts because some accounts may have been legitimate accounts that were compromised via hacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political candidate verification labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter partnered with Ballotpedia to add special labels verifying the authenticity of political candidates running for election in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels serve to verify candidate authenticity to users; this was introduced in response to concerns about malicious use of the platform to influence elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of manipulation policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter removed accounts that violated its manipulation policies and attributed such accounts to organized operations (state-run or otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy enforcement targeted coordinated manipulation (e.g., propaganda, spammy networks); removal counts (tens of thousands) show enforcement scale; attribution and disclosure varied depending on confidence in findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bot identification and distinction between benign vs malicious bots
rubrics_metrics.description: Bots are programs that automatically tweet/retweet/follow; benign bots may generate creative content or product updates, while malicious bots make unpopular people seem popular, push irrelevant products, spread misinformation, spam or slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of bots rests on automated behavior patterns and the platform's open API and cloud infrastructure enabling bots; policy responses differ depending on whether the bot is benign or malicious and on observed impact (e.g., election interference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling and moderation of misinformation (including COVID-19 false medical info)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start of the 2020 COVID‑19 pandemic, Twitter announced new policies to label tweets containing misinformation; historically the platform labeled and removed content judged to be false or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling was used as a mitigation measure rather than outright removal in many cases; enforcement practices changed under different ownership (e.g., elimination of the misinformation moderation team and stopping enforcement of certain labeling under new management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pornographic content allowed if marked 'sensitive'
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter allows pornographic content as long as it is marked 'sensitive' by uploaders, which places it behind an interstitial and hides it from minors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uploaders are responsible for marking sensitive content; features like 'super-follow' were used to monetize adult content, and internal projects explored adult content monetization but faced implementation difficulties (e.g., Real ID).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age verification (Real ID / ID or photo selfie) for sensitive content in UK/EU/EEA
rubrics_metrics.description: X uses Age Verify with ID or Photo Selfie for users to access sensitive content like pornography in the UK, EU and EEA to comply with the Online Safety Act 2023 and EU's Digital Services rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age verification mechanisms were implemented in these jurisdictions to meet legal obligations, reflecting jurisdiction‑specific compliance rather than global policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of child sexual exploitation (CSE) content and reporting limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports indicated Twitter lacked sufficient investment in technologies to detect/manage growing CSE content; until Feb 2022, flagging options were limited (e.g., 'sensitive media'), leaving much illegal content deprioritized for moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal working groups made recommendations to improve CSE detection and prioritization; alleged failures to remove CSE content led to lawsuits and brand ad withdrawals; platform obligations include faster prioritization and better automated detection to scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to deepfake pornography and misuse by integrated AI tools (Grok)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports in Dec 2025 alleged X's chatbot Grok allowed prompts that generated non‑consensual explicit images, including of minors, facilitating sexual abuse, revenge porn and child pornography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such findings prompted legal and regulatory scrutiny, calls for bans, and critiques about product safeguards; the entries cite examples of problematic prompt behavior ('put her in a bikini') and disproportionate targeting of women/girls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship/compliance with government requests and blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: X/Twitter complied with removal requests and was blocked or banned in some countries; the company handled large numbers of legal demands from governments and removed tweets/accounts per those demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter published transparency reports showing legal demand volumes by country; compliance varied and sometimes led to public disputes with governments (e.g., India, Turkey) and temporary national blocks or court orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation/removal of propaganda and coordinated accounts (state actors and political actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter removed tens or hundreds of thousands of propaganda accounts linked to state actors and political parties (e.g., Chinese Communist Party, United Russia, Turkish networks, Saudi‑linked operations, Russian IRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removals were based on detection of centralized/coordinated behavior promoting biased political narratives; Twitter sometimes traced networks across languages and media outlets to assess impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Notes (formerly Birdwatch) crowd‑sourced fact‑checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Birdwatch/Community Notes is a crowd‑sourced moderation tool intended to debunk misinformation, initially launched as a pilot with contributors, later expanded and rebranded to Community Notes with aliasing and randomized viewing/rating of notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program features included contributor aliases to limit bias, randomized sets of users to view and rate notes, expansions to more countries, and tracking contributor activity; success metrics emphasized helpfulness and ability to inform understanding rather than author identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency features for user accounts to combat bots and influence operations
rubrics_metrics.description: In Nov 2025, X began displaying information on user accounts (location, history, username changes) for transparency to combat bots and malicious accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New account metadata aimed to reveal inconsistencies (e.g., claimed location vs displayed data) to help users and researchers identify possible rage farming or foreign influence operations, though it also created controversies over accuracy and privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal liability and adjudication standards involving user-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Court cases examined whether X/Twitter is liable for terrorism-related information and other user content (e.g., Twitter v. Taamneh, Gonzalez v. Google) and raised questions about Section 230 protections and other statutory frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal outcomes (e.g., Supreme Court rulings) affect platform liability exposure and influence how moderation and content‑policy decisions are framed vis‑à‑vis federal statutes like the Antiterrorism Act and Section 230; these adjudications shape enforcement risk and compliance priorities.
